Guided Inquiry

1 · The quantum spring

Let’s get our bearings first. A particle is held by a spring-like force: the parabolic potential V(x) = ½mω²x² in the top panel, with its ladder of allowed energies. Below it you’ll see the wavefunction ψ(x,t) and the probability density |ψ|² — where the particle can be found. The quantum number n selects one allowed state.

2 · The classical oscillator

Let’s warm up with classical physics: a mass on a spring swings back and forth between two extreme points. If you photographed it at many random moments, where do you think it would be found most often?

3 · Beyond the turning points

Now look at the dotted arrows in the top panel. They stop at the turning points, where the energy meets the potential, and a classical mass can never pass them. So what’s your guess? Beyond those points, |ψ|² is…

4 · Towards the classical limit

Here’s a puzzle. The ground state peaks at the centre — the opposite of the classical answer. So climb right up to the highest state, n = 10. Where do you think the tallest peaks of |ψ|² will lie?

5 · Reading the ladder

Now let’s turn to the energies. In the particle-in-a-box, energy levels spread apart as n². Take a careful look at the ladder drawn on this parabola. Going up in n, the gaps between neighbouring levels…

6 · Can the spring rest?

One last puzzle. A classical mass can hang at rest at the bottom of the well with E = 0. But the lowest quantum state, n = 0, still has E₀ = ½ħω. What do you think forbids zero energy?

About Simulation

This simulation models a 1D Quantum Harmonic Oscillator in units where \(\hbar = 1\), with user-controlled mass \(m\) and angular frequency \(\omega\).

  • Harmonic Potential: Displays the parabolic potential \(V(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2x^2\) and the corresponding energy levels.
  • Wavefunction: Visualizes the real and imaginary parts of the time-dependent wavefunction ψ(x,t).
  • Probability Density: Shows |ψ(x,t)|², representing the particle's position probability distribution.

Use the right sidebar to adjust the quantum state n, mass m, and angular frequency \(\omega\) to observe how the eigenstate width and energy spacing change. The animation-speed control only changes how quickly the plotted phase advances on screen.

The Physics

The quantum harmonic oscillator · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A quantum particle held by a spring-like force can only have certain energies, and each one comes with its own wave shape. This sim shows one such state at a time, so you can compare the quantum picture with a classical mass on a spring.

What you'll learn

  • How the allowed energies En depend on n, m and ω.
  • How the shape of ψ and |ψ|² depends on n, and on the length scale that m and ω set.
  • How the quantum density compares with the classical motion between the turning points.
  • What fixes the lowest allowed energy, and how a state's time dependence enters ψ(x, t) and |ψ|².
The model: one particle in the parabola V(x) = ½mω²x². The sim draws one allowed energy at a time, with its two turning points.

What's on screen

  • Top panel, Harmonic Potential & Energy Levels: the purple parabola is V(x). The horizontal lines, labelled n = 0, 1, 2 …, are the allowed energies. The state you chose is blue, with dotted arrows ending at its turning points.
  • Middle panel, Wavefunction ψ(x, t): Re ψ in blue and Im ψ in pink.
  • Bottom panel, Probability density |ψ|²: the green curve.
  • Parameters box: the clock, the state's energy, its turning points ±xtp, and the oscillator length √(ħ/mω).
See itStart from n = 3, with m = ω = 1. Watch for: the blue n = 3 line with its dotted arrows in the top panel, and one curve in each panel below.

03

The well fixes the allowed energies

Inside the well, ψ obeys the Schrödinger equation with V(x) = ½mω²x². There is no fixed width as in a box; instead ψ must die away at large |x|, and that works only at certain energies.

The Equations box: the Schrödinger equation for the parabola.
The allowed energies, with n = 0, 1, 2, … (ħ = 1 in the sim).
  • Equal gaps. En is linear in n, so every neighbouring pair of rungs is ħω apart. In a box, E grows as n² and the gaps widen.
  • The lowest rung is E₀ = ½ħω, not 0. Section 06 shows why.
  • Only ω sets the spacing. The mass m does not appear in En. At ω = 1 the readout is n + ½.
Computed at m = ω = ħ = 1: the parabola, all eleven rungs the n slider reaches (n = 0 to 10), and n = 3 with the turning-point arrows the sim draws in blue.
See itStep n from 0 to 4 and read the Energy each time. Watch for: the Energy readout going up by the same amount at every step, and the blue line climbing one rung at a time.
04

One length sets every state's shape

What the sim's ψn evaluates: a constant, a Hermite polynomial Hn, and a Gaussian.
  • Same Gaussian, different polynomial. The Gaussian e−x²/2x₀² sets the size; Hn adds the wiggles.
  • n zero crossings, n + 1 peaks. ψn crosses zero n times, so |ψn|² has n + 1 peaks. n = 0 is a single hump. Even n gives a symmetric ψ, odd n an antisymmetric one.
  • One length, x₀ = √(ħ/mω). It is the sim's Osc. length readout. Only the product mω enters it, so raising m or ω narrows every curve by the same factor, 1/√(mω).
  • Energy is different. En depends on ω alone. Raising m narrows the wave and leaves E unchanged; raising ω narrows it and raises E.
See itGo to n = 5. Watch for: five zero crossings in the middle panel, and six peaks in the green curve.
See itAt n = 3, raise m to 1.2, then return m to 1 and raise ω to 1.2. Watch for: Osc. length falling to 0.913 both times, while Energy stays 3.50 for m and rises to 4.20 for ω.
05

The tails reach past the turning points

A classical mass with energy En cannot go where V(x) > En. Its turning points ±xtp are where En = ½mω²xtp², the ends of the blue arrows: xtp = √(2n + 1)·x₀.

The sim's ψ and |ψ|² panels at m = ω = 1 on its fixed axes: n = 0 on the left, n = 10 on the right. The amber dashed curve is the classical time-average density for the same energy. It is added here for comparison, and the sim never draws it.
  • The tails go past xtp. ψ falls off like a Gaussian but is not zero beyond the turning points. For n = 0 about 16% of the probability lies there; for n = 10, about 6%.
  • n = 0 is the opposite of classical. A classical mass moves slowest near its ends and lingers there. |ψ₀|² peaks at the centre.
  • Large n looks more classical. At n = 10 the outermost peaks of |ψ|² are the tallest, about twice the central ones, and they sit just inside the turning points. The quantum density oscillates fast around the classical average.
See itGo to n = 0. Watch for: the green curve still above the axis beyond ±1.00, where the blue arrows in the top panel end.
See itGo to n = 10. Watch for: the tallest green peaks at the two ends, just inside ±4.58. The left one is behind this card; the right one is clear.
06

The ground state cannot sit still

Exact rest at the bottom would mean x = 0 and p = 0 together, which Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 forbids. An estimate shows the cost of squeezing either one:

A kinetic term that grows as Δx shrinks, a potential term that grows as Δx grows, and a minimum between them.

The states themselves satisfy this exactly:

Spreads in x and p for state n. Δx and Δp are standard results; the sim does not display them.
n m ω

These sliders move the sim too.

  • n = 0 sits on the bound. Δx Δp = ħ/2 exactly, and the energy is the minimum ½ħω.
  • Higher rungs are further from it. Δx Δp = (n + ½)ħ, which is 2n + 1 times ħ/2.
See itGo to n = 0. Watch for: the Energy readout showing 0.50, not 0.
07

Stationary states have a turning phase

The whole time dependence is one phase factor, and it cancels in |Ψ|².
  • The middle panel is alive. Re Ψ (blue) and Im Ψ (pink) share the shape ψn(x), and the phase moves amplitude between them.
  • The bottom panel is frozen. |Ψ|² = |ψn|² has no t in it. That is what "stationary state" means.
  • Higher rungs turn faster. The phase turns at En/ħ, so at the same ω, n = 10 turns 21 times faster than n = 0.
  • Animation speed is a viewing rate. It scales the on-screen phase only. The energy, the turning points and |ψ|² do not change.
  • A density that really moves, such as a packet sloshing in the well, needs a superposition of several rungs. This sim shows one state at a time.
See itGo to n = 1 at full speed. Watch for: the blue and pink curves trading places in about 4 s per turn, while the green curve stays put.
08

Where it matters

Near any smooth minimum the first surviving term is a parabola, so this one problem appears everywhere.
  • Molecular vibration. The C–O bond has ħω ≈ 0.27 eV, so its stretch absorbs infrared light near 2143 cm⁻¹. Its zero-point energy is about 0.13 eV, and the zero-point spread of the bond length is about 3 pm on a 113 pm bond.
  • Frozen vibration. At room temperature kT ≈ 0.026 eV, a tenth of ħω. A Boltzmann estimate puts about 3 molecules in 100 000 in n = 1, so nearly all sit in n = 0.
  • Helium. Its large zero-point motion and very weak atom-atom attraction keep it liquid at absolute zero unless about 25 atmospheres are applied.
  • Phonons and photons. Each vibration mode of a crystal, and each mode of light in a cavity, has the energies (n + ½)ħω. Here n counts the quanta, and every mode keeps its ½ħω.
Go deeper: a real bond is not exactly a parabola
Carbon monoxide computed from its measured constants (ωe = 2170 cm⁻¹, re = 1.128 Å, De = 11.1 eV): near the minimum the real Morse curve and the parabola agree. The harmonic rungs sit ħω = 0.269 eV apart, with the n = 0 floor at 0.134 eV.
  • Real levels creep closer together higher up the well, which is why the measured 2143 cm⁻¹ is a little below the harmonic 2170 cm⁻¹. This sim models the parabola only, so its rungs stay exactly ħω apart.
09

Summary

In one line. In a parabolic well the allowed energies are En = (n + ½)ħω: evenly spaced, starting half a quantum above zero, with a standing wave of n zero crossings at each rung.

Key points

  • Every gap is ħω, and the lowest energy is ½ħω because Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 forbids exact rest.
  • x₀ = √(ħ/mω) sets the width of every state. Energy depends on ω alone.
  • ψn has n zero crossings, |ψn|² has n + 1 peaks, and the tails reach past the turning points.
  • A stationary state's phase turns at En/ħ, while |ψ|² stays fixed.

Common mix-ups

  • "At n = 0 the particle rests at the bottom with zero energy." Rest would fix x and p exactly, which the uncertainty principle forbids. The floor is ½ħω.
  • "The bottom panel shows the particle oscillating." In one state |ψ|² never changes. Only Re Ψ and Im Ψ move, and they are not probabilities.
  • "The particle is always most likely near the ends, like a classical mass." At n = 0 the density peaks at the centre. The classical pattern appears only as n grows.

Things to try on your own

  • Step n from 0 to 10 and write down each Energy. Then set ω = 0.7 and check the gap again.
  • At n = 10, count the peaks of |ψ|² and compare with n + 1.
  • Set n = 3, m = 1.2 and ω = 0.7. Predict the Energy and the Osc. length, then check the readouts.
